Physiology-01.question: ১) Who introduced the word ‘milieu intérieur’ first?
Physiology-01.exp:
The term milieu intérieur ("internal environment") was first introduced by the French physiologist Claude Bernard in the 19th century. He proposed that the constancy of the internal environment is essential for the survival and proper functioning of cells.

Later, Walter B. Cannon expanded this concept and coined the term "homeostasis" to describe the physiological mechanisms that maintain a stable internal environment.

The other options are incorrect:

  • W.B. Cannon – Introduced the term homeostasis, not milieu intérieur.

  • Poiseuille – Known for Poiseuille's law describing laminar blood flow.

  • Landsteiner – Discovered the ABO blood group system.

Physiology-01.question: ২) Skin generally comprises about what percentage of the body weight?
Physiology-01.exp:
The skin is the largest organ of the human body and accounts for approximately 15–16% of total body weight in an average adult. Besides serving as a protective barrier, it has important roles in:

  • Thermoregulation

  • Sensation

  • Vitamin D synthesis

  • Prevention of water loss

  • Immune defense

The other options are less accurate because the widely accepted value is about 15–16%, making 15–18% the best answer.

Physiology-01.question: ৩) What is the normal value of glucose in ECF in mg/dl?
Physiology-01.exp:
The normal glucose concentration in the extracellular fluid (ECF) is approximately 90 mg/dL (90 mg/100 mL) under fasting conditions. This level is maintained by hormonal regulation, primarily through the actions of insulin and glucagon, to ensure a continuous supply of glucose to tissues, especially the brain.

The other options (65, 75, and 85 mg/dL) are lower than the standard physiological value commonly cited in physiology textbooks.

Physiology-01.question: ৪) What is the another name of adaptive control?
Physiology-01.exp:
Adaptive control is sometimes referred to as delayed negative feedback. In adaptive control, the body learns from previous errors and modifies future responses to improve performance. This mechanism is especially important in motor control, where movements occur too rapidly for immediate feedback correction. The brain uses feed-forward control during the movement and then adjusts subsequent movements based on sensory feedback. Thus, adaptive control is considered delayed negative feedback. 

The other options are incorrect:

  • Delayed positive feedback – Not a recognized physiological control mechanism.

  • Rapid negative feedback – Describes ordinary negative feedback, not adaptive control.

  • Rapid positive feedback – Positive feedback amplifies a response and is unrelated to adaptive control.

Physiology-01.question: ৫) Na⁺-K⁺ pump is an example of which type of transport?
Physiology-01.exp:
The Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase (Na⁺-K⁺ pump) is a classic example of primary active transport because it directly uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to transport ions against their concentration gradients.

For each ATP molecule hydrolyzed, the pump:

  • Extrudes 3 Na⁺ ions out of the cell.

  • Imports 2 K⁺ ions into the cell.

This pump maintains the resting membrane potential, regulates cell volume, and provides the sodium gradient that drives many secondary active transport processes.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Secondary active transport – Uses the energy stored in an ion gradient rather than ATP directly.

  • Co-transport (symport) – Moves two substances in the same direction (e.g., Na⁺-glucose cotransporter).

  • Counter transport (antiport) – Moves two substances in opposite directions using an ion gradient (e.g., Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger), not ATP directly.

Physiology-01.question: ৬) Which organelle is responsible for muscular contraction?
Physiology-01.exp:
Microfilaments are the cytoskeletal elements primarily responsible for muscle contraction. They are composed of actin filaments, which interact with myosin to produce contraction through the sliding filament mechanism. Microfilaments also play important roles in cell movement, cytokinesis, and maintaining cell shape.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Microtubules – Involved in intracellular transport, cilia, flagella, and mitotic spindle formation.

  • Intermediate filaments – Provide mechanical strength and structural support.

  • Ribosomes – Responsible for protein synthesis.

Physiology-01.question: ৭) Which is not one of the five components of protoplasm?
Physiology-01.exp:
The five major components of protoplasm are:

  • Water

  • Electrolytes

  • Proteins

  • Lipids

  • Carbohydrates

These constituents make up the bulk of living cells and are essential for maintaining cellular structure and function.

The other options are components of protoplasm:

  • Carbohydrate – Energy source and structural component.

  • Protein – Principal structural and functional component of cells.

  • Electrolyte – Essential for membrane potential, enzyme activity, and osmotic balance.

Although vitamins are essential for normal cellular metabolism, they are present only in minute amounts and are not considered one of the five major components of protoplasm.

Physiology-01.question: ৮) Which of the following is most important ICF electrolyte in excess?
Physiology-01.exp:
Potassium (K⁺) is the principal intracellular (ICF) cation and is the most abundant electrolyte inside cells. Approximately 98% of total body potassium is located within the intracellular fluid, where it plays a vital role in:

  • Maintaining the resting membrane potential

  • Nerve impulse conduction

  • Muscle contraction

  • Cellular metabolism

The other options are predominantly extracellular (ECF) electrolytes:

  • Na⁺ – Major extracellular cation.

  • Cl⁻ – Major extracellular anion.

  • HCO₃⁻ – Important extracellular buffer anion.

Physiology-01.question: ৯) How many genes are there in each cell?
Physiology-01.exp:
This question reflects the traditional physiology/embryology textbook value, in which each human cell was described as containing approximately 30,000 genes. Older editions of standard textbooks (e.g., Guyton) commonly used this figure for teaching purposes.

However, based on the completed Human Genome Project, the current estimate is that the human genome contains about 20,000–21,000 protein-coding genes.

For examinations based on older physiology texts, the expected answer is 30,000.

Physiology-01.question: ১০) CO₂ is transported from blood to alveoli by which of the following process?
Physiology-01.exp:
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) moves from the pulmonary capillary blood to the alveoli by simple diffusion, driven by the partial pressure gradient. Because CO₂ is highly lipid-soluble (about 20 times more diffusible than O₂), it readily crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane without the need for transport proteins or energy.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Facilitated diffusion – Requires carrier proteins; CO₂ does not require them.

  • Primary active transport – Requires ATP; not involved in gas exchange.

  • Secondary active transport – Depends on ion gradients; not involved in CO₂ transport across the alveolar membrane.

Physiology-01.question: ১১) Which of the following decreases Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase activity?
Physiology-01.exp:
Digitalis (e.g., digoxin) inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase pump in cardiac muscle cells. This results in:

  • ↑ Intracellular Na⁺

  • ↓ Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchange

  • ↑ Intracellular Ca²⁺

  • ↑ Myocardial contractility (positive inotropic effect)

The other options are incorrect:

  • Diuretics – Do not directly inhibit the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase.

  • Insulin – Stimulates Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase activity, promoting K⁺ entry into cells.

  • Glucagon – Does not significantly inhibit the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase.

Physiology-01.question: ১২) When RBCs are suspended in hypertonic solution what they will result?
Physiology-01.exp:
When red blood cells (RBCs) are placed in a hypertonic solution, the extracellular fluid has a higher solute concentration than the intracellular fluid. Water moves out of the RBCs by osmosis, causing the cells to shrink (crenate).

The other options are incorrect:

  • Swell up – Occurs in a hypotonic solution.

  • Hemolysis – Occurs in a hypotonic solution when excessive water enters the RBCs.

  • No change – Occurs in an isotonic solution.

Physiology-01.question: ১৩) Diffusion is inversely proportional to___
Physiology-01.exp:
According to Fick's law of diffusion, the rate of diffusion is:

  • Directly proportional to:

    • Concentration gradient

    • Surface area

    • Temperature

    • Membrane permeability

  • Inversely proportional to:

    • Thickness of the membrane

    • Molecular size/weight (larger molecules diffuse more slowly)

Physiology-01.question: ১৪) Osmotic force depends upon which of the following?
Physiology-01.exp:
Osmotic pressure (osmotic force) depends on the number of osmotically active particles present in a solution, not on their size, molecular weight, or chemical nature. The greater the number of dissolved particles, the greater the osmotic pressure.

This is explained by the van't Hoff equation:

π=iCRTπ=iCRT

where:

  • π = Osmotic pressure

  • i = Number of particles formed after dissociation

  • C = Concentration of particles

  • R = Gas constant

  • T = Absolute temperature

The other options are incorrect:

  • Nature of barrier – A semipermeable membrane is required for osmosis but does not determine the osmotic force.

  • Molecular weight – Osmotic pressure depends on the number of particles, not their molecular weight.

  • Type of substance – The chemical nature is unimportant; only the number of dissolved particles matters.

Physiology-01.question: ১৫) Which of the following contain oxidase?
Physiology-01.exp:
Peroxisomes contain oxidase enzymes (e.g., urate oxidase, D-amino acid oxidase) and catalase. Oxidases generate hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) during oxidation reactions, and catalase rapidly converts H₂O₂ into water and oxygen, protecting the cell from oxidative damage.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Lysosomes – Contain acid hydrolases, not oxidases.

  • Mitochondria – Contain enzymes for oxidative phosphorylation but are not the organelles classically associated with oxidase enzymes in this context.

  • Golgi apparatus – Involved in protein modification, sorting, and packaging.

Physiology-01.question: ১৬) Where does detoxification of drugs occur?
Physiology-01.exp:
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is the principal site of drug and toxin detoxification, particularly in hepatocytes. It contains the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme system, which metabolizes drugs, alcohol, and other xenobiotics.

Other important functions of the SER include:

  • Lipid and steroid synthesis

  • Detoxification of drugs and toxins

  • Calcium storage (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle)

The other options are incorrect:

  • Mitochondria – ATP production and oxidative phosphorylation.

  • Rough ER – Protein synthesis.

  • Peroxisomes – β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids and detoxification of H₂O₂, not the major site of drug metabolism.

Physiology-01.question: ১৭) What cytoskeletal structure connects extracellular matrix to intracellular matrix?
Physiology-01.exp:
Microfilaments (actin filaments) connect the extracellular matrix (ECM) to the intracellular cytoskeleton through integrins at focal adhesions. This linkage:

  • Maintains cell shape

  • Enables cell adhesion and migration

  • Transmits mechanical signals between the ECM and the cell interior

    Focal adhesion → Actin microfilament ↔ Integrin ↔ ECM
    Hemidesmosome → Intermediate filament ↔ Integrin ↔ ECM

The other options are incorrect:

  • Microtubules – Involved in intracellular transport, mitosis, and cilia/flagella.

Physiology-01.question: ১৮) Which is not allowed in acetylcholine gated channel?
Physiology-01.exp:
The acetylcholine-gated (nicotinic) channel is a ligand-gated non-selective cation channel. When acetylcholine binds, the channel opens and allows the passage of:

  • Na⁺ → Enters the cell (major inward current)

  • K⁺ → Leaves the cell

  • Ca²⁺ → Permeable to a lesser extent in some nicotinic receptor subtypes

It does not allow Cl⁻ to pass.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Na⁺ – Passes through the channel.

  • K⁺ – Passes through the channel.

  • Ca²⁺ – Permeable in some nicotinic receptors.

Physiology-01.question: ১৯) Which is the duration of muscle twitch in slow muscle fiber?
Physiology-01.exp:
A muscle twitch is the mechanical response of a muscle fiber to a single action potential.

  • Fast muscle fibers → Twitch duration ≈ 7.5 ms

  • Slow muscle fibers → Twitch duration ≈ 75 ms

Slow fibers have a longer contraction time because of:

  • Slower myosin ATPase activity

  • Slower calcium handling by the sarcoplasmic reticulum

  • Greater resistance to fatigue

The other options are incorrect:

  • 7.50 ms – Fast muscle fiber.

  • 10.00 ms – Too short for slow muscle fibers.

  • 100.00 ms – Longer than the standard value.

Physiology-01.question: ২০) What is the location of RNA in nucleus?
Physiology-01.exp:
The nucleolus is the major site of RNA (especially rRNA) synthesis within the nucleus. It is responsible for:

  • Synthesis of ribosomal RNA (rRNA)

  • Assembly of ribosomal subunits

Although RNA is also present in the nucleoplasm during transcription and processing, the nucleolus is the characteristic nuclear structure richest in RNA and is the expected answer in physiology and cell biology MCQs.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Nuclear membrane – Encloses the nucleus.

  • Nucleoplasm – Contains chromatin and nucleotides but is not the principal site associated with RNA.

  • Chromosome – Mainly composed of DNA and proteins.

Physiology-01.question: ২১) Which of the following can cause hemolysis?
Physiology-01.exp:
Copper can cause hemolysis by producing oxidative damage to the red blood cell membrane, leading to intravascular hemolysis. Acute copper poisoning and severe copper toxicity (e.g., in Wilson disease) are well-known causes of hemolytic anemia.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Zinc – Does not typically cause hemolysis.

  • Lead – Primarily inhibits heme synthesis, causing microcytic hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling, not hemolysis.

  • Chromium – Not a common cause of hemolysis.

Physiology-01.question: ২২) Which is not true about RBC?
Physiology-01.exp:
Normal red blood cells (RBCs) have the following features:

  • Biconcave disc shape ✔️

  • No nucleus in mature RBCs ✔️

  • Thickness: about 2.5 μm at the periphery and 1 μm at the center ✔️

  • Flexible but osmotically fragile ✔️

Therefore, the statement "non fragile" is not true, as RBCs can undergo hemolysis in hypotonic solutions and have measurable osmotic fragility.

The other options are correct:

  • Biconcave – True.

  • No nucleus – True.

  • Thickness 2.5 μm – True (maximum thickness at the periphery).

Physiology-01.question: ২৩) Iron is stored in which form?
Physiology-01.exp:
Ferritin is the major storage form of iron in the body. It stores iron mainly in the:

  • Liver

  • Spleen

  • Bone marrow

Ferritin is a water-soluble protein complex that releases iron when needed.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Transferrin – Transports iron in the plasma; it is not a storage form.

  • Apoferritin – The protein shell of ferritin without iron.

  • Hemosiderin – An insoluble storage form of iron that accumulates when iron stores are excessive; it is a secondary storage form.

Physiology-01.question: ২৪) ‘Cartwheel’ appearance of nucleus is characteristics of which stage?
Physiology-01.exp:
During erythropoiesis, the nucleus becomes progressively smaller and the chromatin becomes increasingly condensed.

Stages of erythroid maturation:

  • Pronormoblast → Large nucleus with fine, delicate chromatin

  • Early (basophilic) normoblast → Chromatin begins to condense

  • Intermediate (polychromatophilic) normoblast → Coarsely clumped "cartwheel" or "checkerboard" chromatin ✔️

  • Late (orthochromatic) normoblast → Small, densely pyknotic nucleus that is eventually extruded

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pronormoblast – Fine chromatin, not cartwheel.

  • Early normoblast – Chromatin condensation has started but is not cartwheel.

  • Late normoblast – Nucleus is pyknotic rather than cartwheel in appearance.

Physiology-01.question: ২৫) Which of the following is the best index of platelet function?
Physiology-01.exp:
Bleeding time (BT) is the best bedside index of platelet function. It assesses:

  • Platelet number (to some extent)

  • Platelet adhesion

  • Platelet aggregation

  • Capillary integrity

Bleeding time is prolonged in conditions such as:

  • Thrombocytopenia

  • Platelet function disorders (e.g., Glanzmann thrombasthenia)

  • von Willebrand disease

  • Aspirin therapy

The other options are incorrect:

  • Clot retraction time – Reflects platelet contractile function but is not the best overall index.

  • Clotting time – Assesses the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, not platelet function.

  • Prothrombin time (PT) – Assesses the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, not platelet function.

Physiology-01.question: ২৬) Which clotting factor is present in both plasma and serum?
Physiology-01.exp:
Serum is the fluid remaining after blood has clotted. During clotting:

  • Fibrinogen (Factor I) is converted to fibrin and is absent from serum.

  • Factors V and VIII are labile and are consumed during coagulation, so they are absent or markedly reduced in serum.

  • Factor VII is a stable clotting factor and is present in both plasma and serum.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Factor VIII – Consumed during clotting; absent from serum.

  • Thrombin (Factor IIa) – Formed transiently during coagulation and is not considered a normal constituent of serum.

  • Factor V – Labile factor; consumed during clotting.

High-yield recall:

  • Absent in serum: Fibrinogen (Factor I), Factor V, Factor VIII

  • Present in both plasma and serum: Factor VII

Physiology-01.question: ২৭) Which is the first factor to be lost from stored blood?
Physiology-01.exp:
During storage of whole blood or packed red blood cells, 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) is the first and most rapidly depleted substance, falling markedly within the first 1–2 weeks of storage. Loss of 2,3-DPG increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, reducing oxygen release to tissues.

The other options are incorrect:

  • ATP – Also decreases during storage, but later than 2,3-DPG.

  • Factor V – A labile clotting factor that decreases in stored plasma but is not the first change in stored blood.

  • Factor VII – A stable clotting factor and is relatively well preserved.

High-yield recall:

  • First to decrease in stored blood: 2,3-DPG

  • Later decrease: ATP

  • Labile clotting factors: V and VIII

Physiology-01.question: ২৮) Essential hormones for erythropoiesis?
Physiology-01.exp:
Thyroxine (T₄) is an important hormone that stimulates erythropoiesis by increasing the body's metabolic rate and oxygen demand, thereby enhancing erythropoietin (EPO) production. Other hormones that promote erythropoiesis include:

  • Erythropoietin (most important)

  • Androgens

  • Growth hormone

  • Cortisol

The other options are incorrect:

  • TSH – Stimulates the thyroid gland but does not directly promote erythropoiesis.

  • Prolactin – Primarily involved in lactation.

  • Estrogen – Does not stimulate erythropoiesis and may even have a mild inhibitory effect.

Physiology-01.question: ২৯) What is the lifespan of average erythrocyte in newborn?
Physiology-01.exp:
The average lifespan of erythrocytes (RBCs) in newborns is about 80 days, which is shorter than in adults because:

  • Neonatal RBCs contain predominantly fetal hemoglobin (HbF).

  • They have greater membrane fragility and are removed more rapidly by the reticuloendothelial system.

High-yield values:

  • Newborn RBC lifespan: ≈ 80 days

  • Adult RBC lifespan: ≈ 120 days

The other options are incorrect:

  • 100 days – Longer than the typical neonatal RBC lifespan.

  • 120 days – Normal lifespan in adults.

  • 140 days – Incorrect.

Physiology-01.question: ৩০) In paracetamol poisoning, what types of jaundice occurs?
Physiology-01.exp:
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causes hepatocellular injury due to accumulation of the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) after depletion of hepatic glutathione. Severe toxicity can lead to:

  • Acute hepatic necrosis

  • Acute liver failure

  • Hepatocellular jaundice

The other options are incorrect:

  • Hemolytic jaundice – Caused by excessive RBC destruction, not paracetamol toxicity.

  • Obstructive jaundice – Due to biliary obstruction, not hepatocellular necrosis.

  • No jaundice – Mild poisoning may not cause jaundice, but clinically significant poisoning typically produces hepatocellular jaundice.

Physiology-01.question: ৩১) ‘Bluish grey’ cytoplasm is the features of which of the following?
Physiology-01.exp:
Monocytes are the largest circulating leukocytes and characteristically have:

  • Abundant bluish-grey (gray-blue) cytoplasm

  • A kidney-shaped or horseshoe-shaped nucleus

  • Fine azurophilic granules and occasional vacuoles

The other options are incorrect:

  • Neutrophil – Pale pink cytoplasm with fine lilac granules.

  • Eosinophil – Large orange-red (eosinophilic) granules.

  • Basophil – Large deep blue-purple granules that often obscure the nucleus.

High-yield recall:

  • Neutrophil → Pale pink cytoplasm

  • Eosinophil → Orange-red granules

  • Basophil → Deep blue-purple granules

  • Monocyte → Bluish-grey cytoplasm

Physiology-01.question: ৩২) Which one is the first line defense against infection?
Physiology-01.exp:
Neutrophils are the first line of cellular defense against infection, especially acute bacterial infections. They are the first leukocytes to migrate to sites of inflammation, where they destroy microorganisms by:

  • Phagocytosis

  • Degranulation

  • Respiratory burst (production of reactive oxygen species)

The other options are incorrect:

  • Macrophage – Important phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells, but they arrive after neutrophils and constitute the second line of cellular defense.

  • Lymphocyte – Responsible for adaptive (specific) immunity.

  • Basophil – Involved in allergic and inflammatory reactions.

High-yield recall:

  • First cellular defense: Neutrophils

  • Second cellular defense: Macrophages

  • Adaptive immunity: Lymphocytes

Physiology-01.question: ৩৩) Which immunoglobulin may act as antigen receptor on the surface of B cell?
Physiology-01.exp:
IgD functions primarily as an antigen receptor (B-cell receptor, BCR) on the surface of mature naïve B lymphocytes. It is co-expressed with surface IgM and plays a key role in B-cell activation when it binds antigen.

The other options are incorrect:

  • IgG – Major immunoglobulin in secondary immune responses and crosses the placenta.

  • IgA – Principal immunoglobulin in mucosal secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk).

  • IgM – Also serves as a B-cell receptor on immature and naïve B cells, but in single-best-answer physiology/immunology MCQs, IgD is classically identified as the immunoglobulin acting as the antigen receptor on mature B cells.

High-yield recall:

  • IgD → B-cell surface receptor

  • IgM → First antibody produced in primary immune response

  • IgG → Most abundant serum antibody; crosses placenta

  • IgA → Secretory (mucosal) antibody

  • IgE → Allergy and parasitic infections

Physiology-01.question: ৩৪) Triple response does not include---?
Physiology-01.exp:
The triple response of Lewis is the characteristic skin response to a firm stroke and consists of:

  1. Red reaction – Appears within a few seconds due to capillary dilatation.

  2. Flare – Surrounding redness caused by arteriolar dilatation mediated by the axon reflex.

  3. Wheal – Localized swelling due to increased capillary permeability and plasma exudation.

The other options are components of the triple response:

  • Red reaction ✔️

  • Flare ✔️

  • Wheal ✔️

White reaction is not part of the classic triple response. It may occur transiently after light stroking due to vasoconstriction but is a separate phenomenon.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৫) What is not fundamental reaction of blood clotting?
Physiology-01.exp:
The fundamental reactions involved in blood clotting are:

  1. Proteolysis – Sequential activation of clotting factors (zymogens) by proteolytic cleavage.

  2. Polymerization – Fibrin monomers polymerize to form the fibrin clot.

  3. Clot formation (clotting) – Formation and stabilization of the fibrin mesh.

The other options are therefore components of the coagulation process.

  • Plasmolysis – Refers to the shrinkage of plant cells due to water loss in a hypertonic solution and has no role in blood coagulation.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৬) Which ion helps in clot retraction?
Physiology-01.exp:
Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) are essential for clot retraction. After a clot forms, platelets contract through their actin-myosin (thrombosthenin) system, pulling on the fibrin strands and causing the clot to retract. This process requires Ca²⁺.

Functions of Ca²⁺ in hemostasis:

  • Essential cofactor in multiple steps of the coagulation cascade (Factor IV).

  • Facilitates platelet contraction during clot retraction.

  • Helps stabilize the fibrin clot.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Mg²⁺ – Not essential for clot retraction.

  • Na⁺ – No specific role in clot retraction.

  • K⁺ – No specific role in clot retraction.

High-yield recall:

  • Factor IV = Ca²⁺

  • Clot retraction requires: Platelets + Fibrin + Ca²⁺

Physiology-01.question: ৩৭) Which is not acquired bleeding disorder due to coagulation defect?
Physiology-01.exp:
von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. It results from a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF), leading to defective platelet adhesion and a secondary reduction in factor VIII activity.

The other options are acquired bleeding disorders due to coagulation defects:

  • Vitamin K deficiency – Decreased synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X.

  • Liver disease – Reduced synthesis of most coagulation factors.

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) – Consumption of clotting factors and platelets.

High-yield recall:

  • Inherited coagulation disorder: von Willebrand disease

  • Acquired coagulation disorders: Vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC

Physiology-01.question: ৩৮) Paternity can be determined from the blood group----?
Physiology-01.exp:
The M & N blood group system has been used in disputed paternity testing (paternity exclusion). Along with the ABO and Rh blood group systems, it can exclude an alleged father if the blood group inheritance is incompatible with Mendelian genetics.

However, blood group testing cannot prove paternity with certainty. Today, DNA analysis is the gold standard for paternity testing.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Kidd – Clinically important in transfusion medicine, not primarily used for paternity testing.

  • Lewis – Blood group system of limited value in paternity testing.

  • Duffy – Important in transfusion medicine and malaria susceptibility, not classically used for paternity testing.

High-yield recall:

  • Classical paternity exclusion: ABO, Rh, M & N blood group systems

  • Definitive paternity test: DNA profiling

Physiology-01.question: ৩৯) Which one is not included in hazards of massive blood transfusion?
Physiology-01.exp:
Massive blood transfusion (replacement of one blood volume within 24 hours or >10 units of packed RBCs) is associated with several well-recognized complications, including:

  • Hyperkalemia – Due to leakage of potassium from stored red blood cells.

  • Citrate toxicity – Citrate binds calcium, causing hypocalcemia (and sometimes hypomagnesemia).

  • Acid–base disturbances – Metabolic acidosis may occur early due to shock and poor tissue perfusion, although metabolic alkalosis can develop later as citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate.

The other options are therefore recognized complications.

  • Thrombophlebitis – This is a complication of intravenous cannulation or infusion, not a characteristic hazard of massive blood transfusion.

High-yield recall:

  • Massive transfusion complications:

    • Hyperkalemia

    • Citrate toxicity → Hypocalcemia

    • Hypothermia

    • Dilutional coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia

    • Acid–base disturbances

Physiology-01.question: ৪০) Which plasma protein responsible for transport of Cu?
Physiology-01.exp:
The major transport protein for copper (Cu) in plasma is ceruloplasmin, which is an α₂-globulin. About 90–95% of plasma copper is bound to ceruloplasmin.

Functions of ceruloplasmin:

  • Transports copper in the blood.

  • Has ferroxidase activity, converting Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, facilitating iron transport by transferrin.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Albumin – Transports a small amount of copper, but it is not the principal transport protein.

  • Fibrinogen – Involved in blood coagulation.

  • Prothrombin – Coagulation factor II.

High-yield recall:

  • Copper transport: Ceruloplasmin (α₂-globulin)

  • Iron transport: Transferrin (β-globulin)

Physiology-01.question: ৪১) The area between two adjacent Z lines is called---?
৪২) The RMP in neuron is---?
Physiology-01.exp:
The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a typical neuron is approximately −70 mV. It is maintained by:

  • High permeability of the membrane to K⁺

  • Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in)

  • Impermeant intracellular anions

High-yield values:

  • Neuron: −70 mV

  • Skeletal muscle: −90 mV

  • Smooth muscle: −50 to −60 mV

The other options are incorrect:

  • −9 mV – Too low.

  • −90 mV – Typical of skeletal muscle, not neurons.

  • −7 mV – Incorrect.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৩) Confirmatory test for diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia does not include---?
Physiology-01.exp:
A peripheral blood film (PBF) is suggestive of iron deficiency anemia but does not confirm the diagnosis. It typically shows:

  • Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs

  • Anisocytosis and poikilocytosis

  • Pencil cells

Confirmatory investigations include:

  • Serum ferritin – Best and most sensitive test for iron deficiency (low in iron deficiency).

  • Serum iron – Decreased.

  • Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) – Increased.

The other options are therefore confirmatory laboratory tests for iron deficiency.

High-yield recall:

  • Best confirmatory test: Serum ferritin ↓

  • Serum iron: ↓

  • TIBC: ↑

  • Transferrin saturation: ↓

Physiology-01.question: ৪৪) In case of DC of WBC monocyte occupies---?
Physiology-01.exp:
In the differential leukocyte count (DLC), monocytes normally constitute 2–8% of circulating white blood cells.

Normal DLC values:

  • Neutrophils: 40–75%

  • Lymphocytes: 20–40%

  • Monocytes: 2–8%

  • Eosinophils: 1–4%

  • Basophils: 0–1%

The other options are incorrect:

  • 20–40% – Lymphocytes.

  • 1–4% – Eosinophils.

  • 0–1% – Basophils.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৫) Dendritic cell is the macrophage present in---?
Physiology-01.exp:
The dendritic cells of the skin are Langerhans cells, which are specialized antigen-presenting cells (APCs) derived from the monocyte–macrophage lineage. They capture antigens in the epidermis and migrate to regional lymph nodes to activate T lymphocytes.

The other options contain different resident macrophages:

  • Spleen → Splenic macrophages

  • Lymph node → Sinus macrophages

  • Liver → Kupffer cells

High-yield tissue macrophages:

  • Skin → Langerhans (dendritic) cells

  • Liver → Kupffer cells

  • Brain → Microglia

  • Lung → Alveolar macrophages

  • Bone → Osteoclasts

Physiology-01.question: ৪৬) Eukaryotic gene does not contain which of the following?
Physiology-01.exp:
A typical eukaryotic gene consists of:

  • Exons – Coding sequences retained in mature mRNA.

  • Introns – Non-coding sequences removed by RNA splicing.

  • Regulatory elements such as promoters, enhancers, and silencers, which regulate gene expression.

A spacer refers to the intergenic DNA that separates adjacent genes on a chromosome. It is not considered part of an individual eukaryotic gene.

The other options are components of a eukaryotic gene:

  • Silencer – Regulatory DNA sequence that suppresses gene transcription.

  • Exons – Coding regions.

  • Introns – Non-coding intervening sequences.

High-yield recall:

  • Eukaryotic gene: Promoter + Exons + Introns + Regulatory elements (enhancers/silencers)

  • Spacer DNA: Intergenic DNA between genes

Physiology-01.question: ৪৭) Bleeding time is prolonged in -----?
Physiology-01.exp:
Bleeding time (BT) assesses primary hemostasis, which depends on:

  • Platelet number

  • Platelet function

  • Vascular integrity

In von Willebrand disease (vWD), deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF) causes defective platelet adhesion, resulting in a prolonged bleeding time.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Hemophilia – Bleeding time is normal because platelet function is normal; aPTT is prolonged.

  • Liver disease – Usually prolongs PT/INR due to reduced synthesis of clotting factors; BT is not characteristically prolonged unless thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction is present.

  • Vascular disease – May cause purpura, but BT is not the classic diagnostic abnormality in this context.

High-yield recall:

  • Bleeding time ↑: von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorders

  • Bleeding time normal: Hemophilia A & B

Physiology-01.question: ৪৮) RBC does not contain which of the following?
Physiology-01.exp:
Mature red blood cells (RBCs) contain several important enzymes required for energy metabolism and protection against oxidative damage, including:

  • G6PD (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) ✔️ – Protects RBCs from oxidative injury by maintaining reduced glutathione.

  • AST (Aspartate aminotransferase) ✔️ – Present within RBCs.

  • LDH (Lactate dehydrogenase) ✔️ – Present in high concentration; serum LDH rises in hemolysis.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is not present in mature RBCs. It is mainly found in:

  • Liver

  • Bone

  • Placenta

  • Intestine

High-yield recall:

  • RBC enzymes: G6PD, LDH, AST, pyruvate kinase, carbonic anhydrase

  • Not present in RBC: ALP

Physiology-01.question: ৪৯) Raised ESR is not found in---?
Physiology-01.exp:
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) increases in conditions associated with increased plasma proteins (especially fibrinogen and immunoglobulins) or reduced hematocrit.

ESR is increased in:

  • Severe anemia ✔️

  • Malignancy ✔️

  • Infections ✔️

Polycythemia is associated with a decreased ESR because the increased red cell mass hinders rouleaux formation and slows sedimentation.

High-yield recall:

  • ESR ↑: Infection, inflammation, anemia, malignancy, pregnancy

  • ESR ↓: Polycythemia, sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis

Physiology-01.question: ৫০) Basophil granule contains all except---?
Physiology-01.exp:
Basophil granules contain several inflammatory mediators, including:

  • Histamine ✔️ – Causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

  • Heparin ✔️ – Acts as an anticoagulant.

  • Bradykinin ✔️ – Basophils can release mediators that contribute to kinin-mediated inflammatory responses, and older physiology texts may list it among basophil mediators.

Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is not a constituent of basophil granules. It is an enzyme found mainly in the azurophilic granules of neutrophils (and to a lesser extent, monocytes), where it helps generate hypochlorous acid for microbial killing.

High-yield recall:

  • Basophil granules: Histamine, Heparin, eosinophil chemotactic factor

  • Neutrophil azurophilic granules: Myeloperoxidase (MPO)
